---
title: "Gini index calculator"
subtitle: "Estimate the Gini index of your own data, with its bias, standard error and confidence interval"
toc: false
html-table-processing: none
---

Paste your data or upload a CSV file to obtain the Gini index with the estimators studied in the project, its **jackknife bias** and **standard error**, a **95% confidence interval** (jackknife and bootstrap), the **Lorenz curve** and, if you choose a grouping variable (for example, sex or region), the **Gini index of each group**.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Your data never leave your computer.** All calculations run in your browser; nothing is uploaded or stored. The jackknife is computed in $\mathcal{O}(n)$ after sorting the data, so it is instantaneous even with hundreds of thousands of observations. For complex survey designs and other intervals (linearisation, empirical likelihood, BCa), use the R package [giniVarCI](software.qmd).
:::

## How to interpret the results

- **$\widehat{G}_n^{b}$** is the usual estimator (equivalently, the Gini index with the mid-point distribution function); **$\widehat{G}_n^{c} = \frac{n}{n-1}\widehat{G}_n^{b}$** is its bias-corrected version; **$\widehat{G}_n^{a}$** is shown for comparison only: it overestimates inequality when inequality is low.
- With **sampling weights**, the weighted estimator $\widehat{G}_{w}$ (mid-point distribution function) is used.
- **Jackknife bias:** estimated bias of the estimator. With small samples or very skewed data the Gini index is usually **underestimated**.
- **Standard error and 95% intervals:** precision of the estimate. Differences between groups, regions or years should be interpreted in the light of these margins of error.
- With sampling weights, the jackknife and the bootstrap delete or resample one unit at a time and ignore the sampling design (strata, clusters); for complex surveys, use `fgini()` in **giniVarCI**.
